### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (low confidence)

The literature review is purposeful, historically deep, and unusually well-integrated with the survey instrument: each construct is traced to a named antecedent, and the three contemporary anchor studies (Koppich & Stipek 2020; Stein & Coburn 2021; Marietta 2010) are described with checkable specifics — sample sizes, page-numbered quotes, and concrete findings. Its blind spots are three: the ECE-leadership evidence it presents is heavily one research team's North Carolina work, the Pre-K effectiveness base is cited only at its most favorable, and the skeptical literature on whether superintendents actually move district outcomes never appears. Readers can trust this paper's characterizations of the studies it cites; they should not treat its picture of the surrounding evidence base as complete.

**Strengths:**

- Genuine archival recovery of the pre-expansion literature. Gallaher, Maddox & Espinosa (1984, Washington state) and Lubeck & Garrett (1989, an ERIC report on North Carolina) are obscure, hard-to-find superintendent surveys, and pulling them forward lets the paper make a substantive point rather than a decorative one: "strong conceptual support, weak enacted support" is a pattern with a 40-year lineage, not a new discovery. This is the most valuable scholarly move in the review.
- Characterizations of the anchor studies are precise and verifiable, which is what a reader most needs. Koppich & Stipek (2020) is reported as 25 California district-leader interviews with 3 of 25 districts seating Pre-K leaders in the cabinet, with a quote at p. 8; Stein & Coburn (2021) is reported as two California districts with three named integrative barriers, with quotes at pp. 845-846; Marietta (2010) is correctly flagged as a Foundation for Child Development policy brief profiling three exemplary superintendents. No case was found where the paper's summary of a cited study exceeded what that study appears to claim.
- The conceptual framework borrows its operationalization honestly rather than inventing one. The regulative/normative/cultural-cognitive scheme is explicitly taken from Stein & Coburn's (2021) application of Scott (2013), and the paper says so and quotes the source. Sensemaking is anchored in the standard education chain (Weick 1995; Coburn 2001; Spillane 2004; Spillane, Reiser & Reimer 2002) rather than a loose gesture at "meaning-making."
- The central-office decision-making literature is engaged in a way that includes evidence cutting against a heroic-leadership premise: Coburn, Toure & Yamashita (2009) on status-quo bias, Honig et al. (2014) on leaders interpreting new ideas to reinforce prior knowledge, and both Trujillo (2012a, 2012b) papers on superintendents limiting deliberation and "pacifying constituents." Many leadership papers cite only the Honig/Bryk optimistic strand.
- The discussion explicitly names a place where its own findings conflict with prior work — superintendents rate their support to principals highly, while Wilinski (2017) finds principals under-engaged with Pre-K and asking for training — and flags it as a triangulation problem rather than resolving it in its own favor.
- Cross-disciplinary borrowing on the methods side is apt and not merely ornamental: Kertzer & Renshon (2022) from political science on surveying political elites, Hendra & Hill (2019) on the weak response-rate/nonresponse-bias link, and RAND's superintendent panel work (Diliberti & Schwartz 2024; Schwartz & Diliberti 2024) are the right sources for defending a 4% response rate.

**Weaknesses:**

- Self-citation concentration is high and, more importantly, geographically concentrated. Little, Cohen-Vogel, or Drake appear on roughly a dozen of the substantive ECE-leadership citations (Little 2020, 2021, 2023; Little & Cohen-Vogel 2016; Little & Gragson 2023; Little et al. 2022, 2025, 2026; Cohen-Vogel et al. 2020, 2022; Drake et al. 2023; Griffard et al. 2022), and the framework's key empirical premise — that ECE background predicts leader investment in Pre-K — rests almost entirely on this team's North Carolina principal studies (Little et al. 2022, 2025; Drake et al. 2023). Brown et al. (2024, Texas) is the main non-NC counterpart cited. This is partly unavoidable in a small subfield these authors largely built, but a reader should not read the framework's empirical warrant as a broad multi-site consensus.
- The paper's central gap claim — "we could find only a handful of studies" and "to our knowledge, this study is the first to explore superintendents' beliefs and practices related to Pre-K education on a nationwide scale" — is asserted without any documented search: no databases, terms, date range, or inclusion criteria. Because the contribution claim rests entirely on this gap, readers have no way to audit it. Notably, two national superintendent survey programs appear in the paper only for methodological or demographic purposes and are never checked for ECE content: Tienken's (2020) AASA decennial American Superintendent study and RAND's American School District Panel (Schwartz & Diliberti 2024). Whether either carries Pre-K items is unknown, but the paper does not tell readers it looked.
- The literature on superintendent effects is engaged only in its optimistic register, and its skeptical quantitative strand is absent entirely. The claim that effective superintendents engage in "authentic reflection" and "group problem solving" rests on Leithwood (1992) — an unpublished AERA conference paper — and Leithwood & Prestine (2002). Absent is the body of work estimating how much superintendents actually explain of district outcomes, which has generally found small or hard-to-detect effects (the Chingos, Whitehurst & Lindquist superintendent value-added work; Waters & Marzano's district-leadership meta-analysis). That literature bears directly on the study's implicit premise that superintendent beliefs about Pre-K matter for what happens in Pre-K classrooms, and its omission is the paper's clearest failure to engage disconfirming evidence.
- The Pre-K effectiveness base is represented by a single 2013 synthesis (Yoshikawa et al.), cited for "improves school readiness skills and a host of later school and life outcomes." The evidence has become substantially more contested since: the Tennessee VPK randomized trial reported null-to-negative effects at third and sixth grade (Lipsey, Farran & Durkin 2018; Durkin et al. 2022), the Head Start Impact Study documented fadeout (Puma et al. 2012), and the 2017 Brookings/Duke consensus statement is the more balanced modern summary. This does not threaten a descriptive leadership survey, but the paper's opening frames the warrant for Pre-K expansion as settled when it is not.
- The gender interpretation outruns its citations. The claim that female superintendents' stronger Pre-K support "reflects the deeply gendered nature of the ECE field" is supported by McDonald, Coles & Thorpe (2024) — a study of how women ECE educators frame the scarcity of men in the workforce — and Schaeffer (2024), a Pew short-read on teacher demographics. Neither is evidence about leaders' policy priorities. The literature on women superintendents' policy agendas and leadership orientations (Grogan & Shakeshaft; Brunner & Grogan) is not engaged. The further inference that "increasing the proportion of female superintendents may increase the emphasis on and effective implementation of ECE" is speculation the cited sources do not license, and the paper itself notes the association appears in only one of three models.
- The "handful of studies on superintendent leadership of ECE" set is defined generously. Of the four works listed in the introduction (Koppich & Stipek 2020; Marietta 2010; Stein & Coburn 2021; Coburn et al. 2018), only Marietta and Koppich & Stipek center district/superintendent leadership as such. Stein & Coburn's two-district study centers P-3 instructional policy across principals and central-office staff; Coburn et al. (2018) is a PACE report on Pre-K-to-elementary alignment in mathematics. Readers should treat only two of the four as true antecedents for the superintendent question.
- Reference-list and naming errors that will impede readers chasing sources. "Wilinksi" is misspelled consistently in text and in the reference list — the author is Bethany Wilinski, and searching the paper's spelling will fail. Scott-Little, Kagan & Frelow (2006) is listed as "Journal of Early Childhood Education, 23(3), 44-56" while carrying an Early Childhood Research Quarterly DOI; the journal name and volume in the entry appear to be wrong (the paper appears in ECRQ 21(2)). The Brown et al. (2024) DOI prefix reads "10.117/" rather than "10.1177/". Stein & Coburn is dated 2021 in text but given as Educational Policy 37(3), a 2023 issue — an online-first/print mismatch readers should be aware of when citing.
- Institutional theory is invoked without its most directly relevant antecedent. The paper's headline finding — near-universal stated support (95% agree Pre-K is critical) alongside weak structural prioritization (38% top-three, 62% no dedicated Pre-K staff) — is close to a textbook case of decoupling formal commitment from operational practice, the core mechanism in Meyer & Rowan (1977). The paper reaches institutional theory through Scott (2013) and Powell & DiMaggio (2012) but never names decoupling, which is the concept that would give its central empirical pattern a theoretical name.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before repeating "the first national study of superintendent leadership of ECE," verify it. Two national instruments cited in this paper for other purposes are the obvious places to check: Tienken (2020), The American Superintendent: 2020 Decennial Study (AASA), and RAND's American School District Panel superintendent surveys (Schwartz & Diliberti 2024). The safest defensible version of the claim is narrower than the paper's: this is the first national survey to make superintendents' Pre-K beliefs, prioritization, and organizational structures its primary subject.
- Read this paper alongside its closest antecedents rather than as a replacement for them. Koppich & Stipek (2020) and Stein & Coburn (2021) supply the causal mechanisms — how blended funding, credentialing mismatch, and misaligned enrollment calendars actually produce the siloing this survey measures. The survey establishes prevalence; the case studies establish process. Neither substitutes for the other, and citing Little et al. for mechanism claims would over-read it.
- Do not use this paper's introduction as a citation for the strength of Pre-K's effects. Yoshikawa et al. (2013) is a 13-year-old synthesis. Pair it with the Tennessee VPK randomized findings (Lipsey, Farran & Durkin 2018; Durkin et al. 2022) and the 2017 Brookings/Duke Consensus Statement on Early Childhood Education for a current view. The paper's descriptive findings about superintendents stand independently of how that debate resolves.
- Discount the causal reading of the gender finding. The claim connecting female superintendents to stronger Pre-K support is (a) present in one of three models, (b) supported by citations about the ECE workforce rather than about leaders, and (c) extended to a policy inference the data cannot bear. For the underlying literature on women superintendents' priorities, go to Grogan and Shakeshaft rather than to McDonald et al. (2024) or the Pew short-read.
- Treat the sensemaking premise — that ECE background predicts leader investment — as North Carolina evidence generalizing untested. Little et al. (2022, 2025) and Drake et al. (2023) are all NC principal studies from this author team. Brown et al. (2024, AERA Open) is the useful Texas counterpart worth reading independently. Note also that this survey did not reproduce the early-grade-teaching-experience association those studies report, which the paper acknowledges but does not dwell on.
- Supply the missing skeptical frame yourself. The superintendent value-added literature (Chingos, Whitehurst & Lindquist) and the district-leadership meta-analytic work (Waters & Marzano) are the counterweight to this paper's premise that what superintendents believe about Pre-K matters downstream. Reading them first changes how much weight to put on the policy implications section.
- For the theoretical frame, go to Meyer & Rowan (1977) on decoupling. The paper's central gap — overwhelming professed support with thin structural investment — is the phenomenon that concept was built to describe, and it is the missing link between this paper's descriptive findings and institutional theory's explanatory apparatus.
- For the mixed-delivery and community-provider dynamics the discussion raises but does not develop, the economics literature is the place to look: Bassok, Fitzpatrick & Loeb on public Pre-K and private-market supply, and Cascio's work on universal Pre-K effects and crowd-out. The paper cites only Little (2020) and Wang et al. (2025, Learning Policy Institute) here, which is thin for a claim about ecosystem-level consequences of district Pre-K expansion.
- On school boards: the paper's most striking descriptive finding is that board prioritization of Pre-K is lowest of all items (25% strongly agreeing), and its explanation — that boards see themselves as representing taxpayers and employers — is offered without any citation. Readers wanting grounding should go to the school-board governance literature (Alsbury; Ford & Ihrke) rather than treating the paper's explanation as evidenced.
- Correct the spelling before searching: the Teachers College Press book cited throughout as "Wilinksi (2017)" is Bethany Wilinski, When Pre-K Comes to School. It is one of the more useful companion reads here, since it documents from the ground the workforce and partnership tensions this survey measures only through superintendents' self-reports.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Assessment scope and uncertainty. This assessment is based on a PyMuPDF text extraction, so Figure 1 (the merged conceptual framework heuristic), which is the visual carrier of the sensemaking/institutional integration, could not be inspected; the judgment of that integration rests on the prose description alone. The supplementary appendices were also unavailable, one of which contains the full instrument — item wording would let a reader judge how faithfully the cited constructs were operationalized, and that cannot be checked here.

On the reviewer's limits: the sensemaking and institutional-theory literatures in education administration are well covered here, and the Pre-K effectiveness and superintendent value-added literatures well enough to be confident those are real omissions. The ECE-leadership subfield specifically — principal and district leadership of Pre-K, P-3 alignment governance — is known considerably less well, and it cannot be ruled out that a paper not known to this reviewer already conducted a national superintendent ECE survey. The reference-detail flags are of uneven confidence: the Wilinski misspelling and the Brown et al. DOI truncation are visible in the text and certain; the Scott-Little journal/volume mismatch is moderately confident and a reader should verify rather than take it on trust.

On the overall verdict. What distinguishes this literature review from a merely competent one is that it does work rather than decorating. The Gallaher (1984) and Lubeck & Garrett (1989) recovery is not padding — it produces the paper's most interesting interpretive claim, that superintendents' conceptual-support-without-prioritization pattern has survived four decades and a complete transformation of Pre-K's institutional position. Likewise the construct-to-citation mapping in the Survey subsection is genuinely traceable, so a reader can see which prior finding each block of items was built to interrogate. And the paper is willing to report a conflict with prior work (superintendents' self-rated support to principals vs. Wilinski's principals) rather than smoothing it.

What holds it at "adequate" rather than "strong" is that the review is optimized to establish a gap rather than to map an evidence base. Three consequences follow for readers. First, the empirical warrant behind the sensemaking half of the framework is narrower than it reads — largely this team's North Carolina principal studies — so the framework's plausibility and its evidentiary support should be assessed separately. Second, the paper never confronts the possibility that superintendent beliefs are weakly connected to what happens in classrooms, which is the standing finding of the quantitative superintendent-effects literature and the most consequential unaddressed challenge to the study's rationale. Third, the gap claim itself is unaudited; for a paper whose contribution is definitionally a gap-filling claim, that is the place a reader most needs a documented search and does not get one.

A note on what the paper does not oversell. The novelty claims in the contributions list are mostly well calibrated — nationwide scope, joint sensemaking/institutional framing, and background-to-outcome associations are all fairly claimed. The one soft claim is that superintendent "views of the goals and purposes of Pre-K" are "heretofore unexplored." School readiness beliefs is a developed literature; the paper itself cites Hustedt et al. (2018) on kindergarten teachers' readiness beliefs and Scott-Little, Kagan & Frelow (2006) on readiness definitions, and there is more (Wesley & Buysse; Piotrkowski et al.). What is new is the population, not the construct — readers should credit the paper for surveying superintendents, not for originating the question.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The prose is clear, well signposted, and easy to navigate: the same four survey domains (beliefs, prioritization, structure, practices) are carried consistently from the abstract through the purpose statement, the survey-construct list in Methods, and the Findings headers, and the exploratory models are hedged repeatedly and explicitly. Fidelity to the exhibits is weaker: significance markers in Tables 1-3 are internally inconsistent (in one case a coefficient one-third the size of its own standard error carries a marginal-significance flag), the Discussion reports coefficients and a headline percentage that appear nowhere in the tables or Findings, and the direction of the two rank-order outcome scales is never defined. A reader can trust the shape of the descriptive story but should re-derive any specific number before quoting it.

**Strengths:**

- Consistent architecture: the four survey domains are stated identically in the abstract (p. 1), the purpose paragraph (pp. 8-9), the survey-development section (pp. 9-10), and the Findings headers (pp. 13-17), so a reader can move between sections without re-orienting.
- Unusually disciplined hedging of the exploratory models. The Analysis section (p. 12) states up front that "individual coefficients should be interpreted as exploratory conditional associations," the opening of the exploratory Findings (p. 18) repeats it, and Limitation 3 (p. 28) returns to it with an explicit power argument. Null results are correctly framed as inconclusive rather than as evidence of no relationship (p. 19).
- The sample-quality discussion (pp. 10-11) is candid and specific: 4% response rate named plainly, the AAPOR basis given, state-level coverage quantified (42 states within +/-2 pp; California underrepresented by 4.67 pp; Kansas overrepresented by 2.64 pp; nine states and DC with zero respondents), and a completer/non-completer comparison reported. The paragraph on p. 11 explicitly restricts inference to "patterns within this group of respondents."
- Descriptive Findings are internally coherent where they can be checked: the six first/second percentages for Pre-K outcomes (p. 14) sum to 201%, exactly the ~200% required when each respondent contributes two ranks, and the Discussion's "62% [of districts have] no dedicated staff member" (p. 26) is the correct complement of the "~38%" reported on p. 16.
- The Discussion does real interpretive work rather than restating results, and the conceptual framework (sensemaking for individual predictors, institutional theory for district predictors) is actually used to organize both the table columns and the Discussion's conceptual-versus-enacted-support split.

**Weaknesses:**

- SIGNIFICANCE MARKERS ARE NOT RELIABLE. Table 2 (p. 20), SEL column, City: the coefficient is -0.19 with a standard error of 0.63 (t = 0.30) yet carries the "~" marker, and the text (p. 20) reports it as a finding ("city superintendents rank this outcome lower [-0.19/6 points]"). No rounding of the standard error can make that estimate distinguishable from zero. Table 3 (pp. 21-22), Percent IEP: Model C is -0.06 (0.02) with NO marker while Model D is -0.06** (0.02) — identical coefficient and identical standard error, contradictory flags. Table 3 Model D, Moderate training: 0.63 (0.26) is t = 2.42 (p ~ .016) but is flagged ** (p < .01). Table 2 SEL, Extensive training: 1.12 (0.58) is t = 1.93 but is flagged * (p < .05). Table 1 (p. 19) Ready, Suburb: 0.23 (0.12) is t = 1.92 but is flagged *.
- The text asserts findings from unflagged cells. Table 1, Special education column: Limited training is -0.39 (0.20) with no significance marker while Moderate training is -0.39~ (0.22) — the more precisely estimated of the two identical coefficients is the unflagged one — yet the text (p. 18) reports both together: "approximately -0.39 for both limited and moderate training." Conversely, several unflagged cells have t-ratios above 2 that go entirely unmentioned, e.g., Table 2 Literacy, student enrollment, -0.03 (0.01), and Table 3 Model C, Percent IEP, -0.06 (0.02).
- COEFFICIENTS REPORTED IN THE TEXT THAT DO NOT APPEAR IN ANY TABLE. The Model E paragraph (p. 21) reports that centralized Pre-K leadership is less likely as the share of multiracial (-11 percentage points/unit) or American Indian (-10 percentage points/unit) students rises. Table 3 contains no racial/ethnic composition rows; the table note says only that models "also adjust for district student racial/ethnic composition." These two estimates — which the Discussion treats as substantively interesting — are unverifiable from the published exhibits. The same applies to every racial/ethnic coefficient in Tables 1 and 2.
- THE DIRECTION OF THE RANKING SCALES IS NEVER DEFINED. The descriptives (pp. 13-14) speak of respondents "ranking it first," implying 1 = most important. But the regression text consistently reads positive coefficients as higher priority ("ranked this purpose higher [approximately +0.23]", p. 18) and negative coefficients as lower priority ("-0.39" = "lower prioritization"). That only works if the outcome is reverse-coded (5 or 6 = most important), which is stated nowhere in the Analysis section (p. 12), the Findings, or the table notes. Every sign in Tables 1 and 2 is therefore uninterpretable at face value without an assumption the paper never supplies.
- A KEY DISCUSSION STATISTIC IS ABSENT FROM THE FINDINGS. The Discussion (p. 23) contrasts "83% of superintendents strongly agreed that Pre-K is critical to their district's educational success" with "only 38% strongly agreed that it ranks among their top three strategic priorities." The Findings (p. 15) never report 83%; they report 95% who "strongly agreed" OR "agreed" with that same item. A reader working only from the Findings would form the comparison 95% vs. 38% — an agree-plus-strongly-agree figure against a strongly-agree-only figure — which is not the contrast the argument rests on. Similarly, the Discussion's "43% ranking language and literacy first and 34% ranking social and emotional development first" (p. 24) are first-place-only figures that never appear in the Findings, which gave only first/second combined (71% and 56%, p. 14).
- THE GENERALIZATION CLAIMS OUTRUN THE PAPER'S OWN STATED LIMITS. Methods (p. 11): findings "should be interpreted as reflecting patterns within this group of respondents rather than as representative of U.S. districts or superintendents nationally." Limitations (p. 28): "it is not nationally representative of all school district superintendents." But the Discussion states that the case-study dynamics "are not limited to particular states or communities but instead characterize superintendent leadership more broadly" (p. 23) and that the study demonstrates "these patterns are evident nationwide" (pp. 27-28). The title ("A National Survey") and the abstract ("nationally distributed survey") sit on the permissive side of that tension, and the abstract carries no representativeness caveat and no mention of the 4% response rate.
- AN INTERNAL CONTRADICTION IN THE GENDER PARAGRAPH (p. 26). Two sentences apart, the paper says the female-superintendent finding "was only present for views on the importance of Pre-K, not models predicting district Pre-K efficacy or the extent to which Pre-K is centrally organized" — and then concludes that "increasing the proportion of female superintendents may increase the emphasis on AND EFFECTIVE IMPLEMENTATION of ECE in districts." The second half of that conclusion is exactly the association the preceding sentence disclaims (Table 3, Model D, Male = -0.21, SE 0.21, unflagged), and it converts an exploratory cross-sectional association into a policy-lever claim.
- The regression tables report no sample size, no R-squared, and no model fit statistics, and the descriptive percentages in Findings live entirely in Figures 2-6 with no accompanying table — so a reader cannot check any descriptive number against tabulated values. The sample-description exhibits (superintendent demographics and background, national vs. sample comparisons, state coverage, completer/non-completer tests) are all in online Appendices B-E rather than the article.
- Denominator ambiguity on pp. 16-17. After reporting that "~38% of superintendents reported that their district had a supervisor of ECE where that is their primary job responsibility," the text says "57% of THESE Pre-K directors are part of the superintendent's senior leadership team, and 81% are a part of regular district leadership meetings" — but it is not stated whether "these" means the ~38% subset or all districts with any Pre-K leader. That matters, because Model E's binary outcome (p. 21) is defined as the conjunction of both conditions, so its base rate is somewhere near 22% if the 57% is conditional on the 38%. The base rate is never reported, which makes the "+26 percentage points" for city districts hard to size.
- Small copy-level lapses survived production: "35.9% female" plus "64.2% male" sums to 100.1% (p. 13); two opening quotation marks are never closed in the outcomes paragraph (p. 14); "strong agreed" for "strongly agreed" (p. 15); an ungrammatical possessive in "Superintendents' from suburban districts support for Pre-K" (p. 26); "have een more likely" (p. 28); and the female share of superintendents is given as ~28% on p. 13 (via "about 72% are male") and 29% on p. 26.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read the Methods sample paragraphs (pp. 10-11) BEFORE the Findings, and read them as the paper's own scope statement. The sentence on p. 11 restricting inference to "patterns within this group of respondents" is the honest framing; the Discussion's "evident nationwide" language (pp. 23, 27-28) is not. When the two conflict, the Methods sentence is the one the design supports.
- Treat the descriptive Findings (pp. 13-17, Figures 2-6) as the load-bearing contribution and the exploratory regressions (pp. 18-21, Tables 1-3) as hypothesis-generating. The authors say this themselves in three separate places, and it is the correct way to read the paper.
- Do not quote a significance level from Tables 1-3 without recomputing it. Divide the coefficient by its standard error yourself: several markers are off by a tier in both directions, and at least one flagged cell (Table 2, SEL, City: -0.19 with SE 0.63) cannot be significant at any conventional level. The corresponding sentence on p. 20 should be disregarded.
- Before citing any sign from Tables 1 or 2, resolve the ranking-direction question — ideally from the survey instrument in online Appendix A. The paper never states whether a higher value means a higher or a lower priority, and the descriptive prose ("ranking it first") points the opposite way from the regression prose ("+0.23 ... ranked this purpose higher").
- If you want to cite the study's signature "strong support but not a top priority" gap, cite the Discussion's paired figures (83% strongly agreed Pre-K is critical vs. 38% strongly agreed it is a top-three priority, p. 23), not the Findings' 95% (p. 15). The 95% is agree-plus-strongly-agree and is not comparable to the 38%.
- Do not cite the multiracial (-11 pp) or American Indian (-10 pp) estimates on p. 21. Those coefficients are not printed in Table 3 or anywhere else in the article, so there is no standard error, no significance level, and no way to judge them; the authors' own cautionary sentence about "smaller base rates implied for some demographic groups" is the relevant signal.
- In the gender paragraph (p. 26), stop at the sentence beginning "That said, this finding was only present for views on the importance of Pre-K." The policy inference in the following sentence — that more female superintendents would improve "effective implementation" of ECE — is contradicted by that very sentence and by Table 3's null Model D gender coefficient.
- Skimmable: the Conceptual Framework and Related Literature (pp. 3-9) is a competent but conventional review; a reader already familiar with Stein and Coburn (2021), Koppich and Stipek (2020), and Marietta (2010) can go straight from the Introduction to Methods. The three-paragraph institutional-theory exposition (pp. 6-7) is largely a summary of Stein and Coburn.
- Do not skim: the Analysis section (p. 12), which names the five outcome constructs and the common predictor set — it is the only place the composite outcomes (Models C and D) are defined at all, and the definition is one clause long; and Limitations (pp. 28-29), which contains the underpowered-models caveat that governs how much weight any table entry can bear.
- If you need the sample's characteristics — who these 404 superintendents are and how their districts compare with the national population — you must go to online Supplementary Appendices B through E. None of that is in the printed article, including the basic demographic table for the sample.
- Note what the regression tables omit: no N, no R-squared, no fit statistics, and no racial/ethnic composition coefficients despite the note saying models adjust for them. Any replication or meta-analytic use of these estimates will require contacting the authors.

**Detailed Commentary:**

SIGNIFICANCE-MARKER AUDIT (coefficient / standard error = implied t; markers as printed). Because standard errors are rounded to two decimals, t-ratios near 1.96 are not decisive on their own — but several discrepancies below are far too large for rounding to explain.

Table 1 (p. 19): Ready/Principal of Pre-K 0.15~ (0.09), t=1.67 — consistent. Ready/Suburb 0.23* (0.12), t=1.92 — flagged p<.05 though t is below 1.96; borderline, rounding could explain. Special education/Limited training -0.39 with NO marker (0.20), t=1.95; Special education/Moderate training -0.39~ (0.22), t=1.77 — the two coefficients are identical, the unflagged one is MORE precisely estimated than the flagged one, and the text on p. 18 reports both as findings. Childcare/City 0.42~ (0.24), t=1.75 — consistent, matches text. Childcare/Percent IEP 0.02~ (0.01), t=2.0 — matches text.

Table 2 (p. 20): Literacy/Moderate -0.58~ (0.32) and Literacy/Extensive -0.74~ (0.41) — both t~1.8, consistent, and correctly reported at pp. 18-19. Literacy/City 1.37** (0.45), t=3.04 — consistent. Literacy/Suburb 0.57* (0.28), t=2.04 — consistent. Cognition/Suburb 0.61~ (0.36), t=1.69 — consistent. Physical/City 0.91~ (0.49), t=1.86 — consistent. Motor/Suburb -0.67* (0.32), t=2.09 — consistent. SEL/Extensive 1.12* (0.58), t=1.93 — flagged p<.05 on a t below 1.96. SEL/City -0.19~ (0.63), t=0.30 — THIS CANNOT BE RIGHT. The standard error is more than three times the coefficient. The text on p. 20 nonetheless reports it: "city superintendents rank this outcome lower (-0.19/6 points)." Also unflagged but large: Literacy/enrollment -0.03 (0.01), t=3.0, and Physical/Limited training -0.56 (0.32), t=1.75, the latter having the same t-ratio as cells flagged "~" elsewhere in the same table.

Table 3 (pp. 21-22): Model C Moderate training 0.49* (0.24), t=2.04 — consistent, matches text p. 21 and p. 25. Model C Male -0.35* (0.16), t=2.19 — consistent. Model C Suburb -0.58** (0.21), t=2.76 — consistent, and the Discussion's "nearly 60% of a standard deviation" (p. 26) is a fair gloss. Model D Moderate training 0.63** (0.26), t=2.42, p~.016 — flagged p<.01 when the implied p is between .01 and .05. Model D Percent IEP -0.06** (0.02), t=3.0 — consistent, matches text p. 21. Model C Percent IEP -0.06 (0.02) with NO marker — identical coefficient and standard error to the Model D cell that is flagged **, and unmentioned in the text. Model E City 0.26~ (0.15), t=1.73 — consistent with the text's "+26 percentage points."

NET: of roughly twenty flagged or borderline cells, at least five carry markers that do not follow from the printed coefficient/standard-error pair, and two identical coefficient/SE pairs carry contradictory flags. This is a production-level failure, not a stylistic one, and it means the printed asterisks cannot be used as-is.

TEXT-TABLE CROSSWALK OTHERWISE. Every other coefficient quoted in the Findings text does appear in the tables with the stated magnitude and sign — the transcription of numbers is accurate; it is the inferential annotation and the omitted rows that fail. The one class of exception is Model E's racial-composition estimates (-11 pp multiracial, -10 pp American Indian, p. 21), which have no table entry at all.

ABSTRACT FIDELITY. The abstract's four findings each map onto something the paper shows: limited ECE experience and training (6% ever taught Pre-K, ~32% taught anywhere in Pre-K-3, 56% reporting no or limited training, p. 13); strong valuation of Pre-K for kindergarten readiness (78% ranked it first, p. 13); general support with varying prioritization (95% agree/strongly agree it is critical vs. 25% strongly agreeing it is a school-board priority, p. 15); and Pre-K leadership embedded in broader roles (~62% of districts with no dedicated ECE staffer, pp. 16-17, 26). The abstract does not overstate the findings' content. What it omits is the strength of the evidence: the 4% response rate, the nine states and DC with zero respondents, and the paper's own statement that the sample is not nationally representative. It also omits the exploratory regressions entirely, which is defensible — those are the least reliable part of the paper — but means an abstract-only reader will not know that the training, gender, and locale correlates exist or how tentative they are. Set against the title's "A National Survey" and the abstract's "nationally distributed survey," the omission tilts an abstract-only reading toward more national authority than the design supports.

ORGANIZATION. The paper is easy to navigate. The four-domain spine holds from abstract to Findings. Within the Findings, the descriptive subsections (pp. 13-17) and the exploratory subsections (pp. 18-21) are cleanly separated, and each exploratory subsection is keyed to a specific table and model letter. The Discussion reorganizes around conceptual versus enacted support rather than around the four domains, which costs a little cross-referencing but earns a more interesting argument. Figure 1 (p. 4) is explicitly disclaimed as a heuristic rather than a causal model (p. 5) — a useful and honest signpost that many papers omit. The regression equation on p. 12 is unreadable in the text extraction, which is an artifact and not the authors' doing; the accompanying prose describes the specification adequately without it.

WHAT THE EXHIBITS CARRY. The paper's contribution is descriptive and lives in Figures 2-6, none of which could be checked here. Tables 1-3 carry the exploratory correlates, and they are the exhibits with the fidelity problems. A reader who takes the descriptive figures at face value and treats Tables 1-3 as a list of hypotheses will come away with an accurate picture; a reader who quotes an asterisk from Table 2 or a percentage-point estimate from p. 21 may not.

RATING RATIONALE. The writing itself is clear, the structure is genuinely helpful, and the authors hedge the weakest analyses more conscientiously than is typical. But this is a published article, and the significance markers in all three tables are unreliable, the Discussion quotes numbers and coefficients a reader cannot find, the ranking scales' direction is undefined, and the generalization language contradicts the paper's own Methods and Limitations. Those are trust-affecting rather than stylistic, and they place the exposition at adequate rather than strong.

CAVEATS ON THIS ASSESSMENT. Bold formatting was lost in extraction, so the audit relied on the printed tilde/asterisk suffixes; if the bolding and the suffixes disagree in the published PDF, some of the marker discrepancies above could resolve differently, though the SEL/City cell (t=0.30) and the identical-but-differently-flagged Percent IEP pair in Table 3 would remain problems under any bolding scheme. Figures 2-6 were unavailable, so all descriptive percentages in the Findings and the 83%/43%/34% figures in the Discussion were checked only against the text itself, not against their source exhibits.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This paper delivers the first nationally distributed survey of U.S. school district superintendents focused specifically on Pre-K and early childhood education, filling a real gap in a literature that had been almost entirely small-sample case studies (Marietta 2010; Koppich & Stipek 2020; Stein & Coburn 2021) or four-decade-old state surveys (Gallaher et al. 1984; Lubeck & Garrett 1989). Its durable contribution is descriptive: a broad-brush portrait of superintendents' stated beliefs about Pre-K's purposes and outcomes, the conceptual-support-versus-strategic-priority gap, and how districts locate Pre-K leadership on the org chart. Its inferential contribution is thin — a 4% response rate on a self-reported instrument, plus roughly 200 exploratory OLS coefficients across three tables, means the correlates the paper is most likely to be quoted for (ECE training, gender, suburban locale) are hypothesis-generating rather than findings the field should build on.

**Strengths:**

- Genuine and well-identified gap. Superintendents are the one leadership tier the ECE-leadership literature had left almost untouched, despite being formally accountable for the Pre-K classrooms that have spread to ~60% of public elementary schools. The paper's framing of that gap is accurate, and the prior-work review (Marietta, Koppich & Stipek, Stein & Coburn, plus the 1980s surveys) is fair rather than strawmanned.
- Infrastructure-based novelty. Fielding through the National Longitudinal Superintendent Database means a near-census sampling frame (9,985 viable emails covering ~79% of the 12,572 districts) rather than a convenience list or an association membership roster. That is a real methodological upgrade over how superintendent surveys are usually assembled, and it is what makes the "national" framing defensible in design even where it is not defensible in realized sample.
- The most substantively interesting result is also one of the best supported descriptively: the conceptual-versus-enacted support gap. Near-universal endorsement that Pre-K is "critical" (95% agree/strongly agree) sits alongside only 38% strongly agreeing ECE is a top-three strategic initiative and 25% saying it is a top school-board priority. Because this is a within-respondent contrast, it is far more robust to nonresponse than any level estimate — a superintendent who overstates support on one item overstates it on both, so the gap survives the bias that eats the levels.
- Genuinely new terrain the prior literature had not touched at all: superintendent rank-orderings of the goals and purposes of Pre-K. The finding that "providing childcare for working families" is ranked last or second-to-last by 94% of respondents, while kindergarten readiness is ranked first by 78%, is a striking and citable descriptive fact about how district leaders construe what Pre-K is for — and it connects productively to the McCabe & Sipple / Wilinski line of work on half-day scheduling and childcare gaps.
- The organizational-structure descriptives (roughly 38% report a supervisor whose primary responsibility is ECE; among those, 57% sit on the senior leadership team and 81% attend regular district leadership meetings) quantify at national scale what Koppich & Stipek could only observe in 25 California interviews. This is the section where the paper most clearly converts case-study intuition into a number.
- Unusually disciplined self-labeling of the inferential work. The paper repeatedly and explicitly calls the regressions exploratory, tells readers that both null and significant coefficients are tentative, invokes Lakens et al. and Tukey, notes the models are underpowered, declines to make state-level claims, and states outright that findings "should be interpreted as reflecting patterns within this group of respondents rather than as representative of U.S. districts or superintendents nationally." Many papers with this design would not say that.
- Nonresponse diagnostics go beyond the minimum: CCD-linked comparison of respondent districts to the national population, state-by-state coverage comparison, and a completer-versus-non-completer comparison. Robustness checks (ordered logit for rankings, logit for the binary outcome, VIF and collinearity sensitivity) are reported.

**Weaknesses:**

- The headline generalization claim contradicts the paper's own methods section. The Discussion asserts that the case-study dynamics "are not limited to particular states or communities but instead characterize superintendent leadership more broadly" and that "these patterns are evident nationwide" — but Methods states the findings reflect "patterns within this group of respondents rather than as representative of U.S. districts or superintendents nationally." Both sentences cannot be cited. The Methods sentence is the correct one; the Discussion sentence is the one that will get quoted.
- A 4% response rate makes every level estimate — the 95% agreement, the 62% without dedicated Pre-K staff, the 78% ranking kindergarten readiness first — vulnerable to topic-salience selection that the CCD covariate balance cannot detect. Superintendents who care about Pre-K are the ones who answer a survey about Pre-K. Balance on enrollment, FRPL, and locale says nothing about balance on ECE interest, which is precisely the latent variable driving every outcome here. The paper cites Hendra & Hill for the proposition that response rates are not reliable indicators of nonresponse bias; that literature says low rates do not *guarantee* bias, not that observable-covariate balance rules it out on a topic-selected outcome.
- The multiple-comparisons arithmetic is unfavorable and never confronted. Tables 1-3 present on the order of 200 coefficients across 14 outcomes. At alpha = 0.05 one would expect roughly 9-10 significant coefficients by chance alone; the tables report a comparable number of starred results, many of them at the ~p<0.10 tier. The paper's exploratory framing is the right posture but is not a substitute for telling readers that the significant-coefficient count is close to the chance baseline.
- The rank-ordered outcomes are ipsative and the paper interprets them as if they were not. Ranking six outcomes means raising one necessarily lowers another, so "ECE training predicts lower literacy ranking and higher SEL ranking" is partly one movement described twice, not two independent findings. Coefficients within a rank battery are mechanically negatively coupled; readers should treat these as statements about relative ordering, never about how much a superintendent values literacy.
- The gender finding carries the paper's largest interpretive leap on its thinnest evidence. From a single coefficient (male -0.35 SD, p<0.05) on one self-reported attitudinal composite, the Discussion reaches "increasing the proportion of female superintendents may increase the emphasis on and effective implementation of ECE in districts." The word "implementation" is unsupported: the paper itself notes the coefficient is absent in the efficacy model and the centralized-organization model, i.e., it appears only for stated beliefs and vanishes for everything resembling enactment. Compounding this, women are overrepresented in the sample (35.9% vs ~28-29% in the NLSD population), so the gender variable is entangled with the selection process.
- Self-report with no triangulation, on constructs where self-report is weakest. Superintendents rating whether their own district effectively supports Pre-K, and whether they support principals as ECE leaders, is measurement of professional self-presentation as much as of district practice — and the paper itself flags that its favorable self-ratings sit "in some contrast to prior research" finding principals under-supported and under-engaged (Wilinski 2017). When self-report and independent observation disagree, that is evidence about the instrument, not just an open question.
- The training correlates are non-monotonic in a way the discussion smooths over. On the importance composite it is *moderate* training that is significant (+0.49 SD), while extensive training (+0.33) is not; on the efficacy composite the same pattern holds (moderate +0.63**, extensive +0.38 n.s.). A genuine dose-response relationship would not peak in the middle and fade at the top. The narrative "training may be a key lever to move the needle" — which then supports a concrete policy recommendation about superintendent professional learning — reads the pattern as monotonic when the coefficients are not.
- Reverse causality is unaddressed for the mechanism the paper most wants to claim. Superintendents who already value ECE are the ones who elect to seek ECE professional development. The training-to-beliefs arrow is at least as plausible in the other direction, and with cross-sectional data there is no leverage to separate them.
- Two internal reporting inconsistencies readers will trip on: the Findings section reports 95% "strongly agreed or agreed" that Pre-K is critical, while the Discussion reports 83% "strongly agreed" for what appears to be the same item, and neither the 83% nor the 43%/34% first-place rankings cited in the Discussion appear in the Findings text. Anyone quoting a specific percentage should verify it against the figures and appendices rather than the Discussion prose.
- The composite outcomes (importance of Pre-K, district Pre-K efficacy) are standardized indices whose item composition and internal-consistency reliability are not reported in the main text. Effect sizes expressed in standard deviations of an unvalidated composite are hard to interpret and hard to compare to anything.
- Design-level silence on state policy context. Whether a state has universal Pre-K, where Pre-K governance sits, and how Pre-K is funded are plausibly the dominant determinants of what a superintendent can and does do — and none of it is in the models, which include only superintendent demographics and district CCD covariates. Given nine states plus DC returned zero respondents and California is underrepresented by 4.67 points, unmodeled state policy is both a large omitted variable and unevenly sampled.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR the existence and shape of the conceptual-versus-strategic-priority gap: superintendents overwhelmingly endorse Pre-K as important while far fewer treat it as a top-three district initiative or a school-board priority. This within-respondent contrast is the paper's most robust result because respondent self-selection inflates both sides of the comparison roughly equally.
- CITE IT FOR the descriptive claim that superintendents construe Pre-K primarily as kindergarten preparation and secondarily as special-education identification, and almost never as childcare for working families. This is new terrain — no prior study asked superintendents to rank Pre-K's purposes — and the 94% ranking childcare last or second-to-last is too lopsided to be an artifact of who answered.
- CITE IT FOR the existence of the shared-responsibility staffing model — that Pre-K leadership is frequently folded into a role with other duties rather than held by a dedicated ECE administrator. This confirms at broader scale what Koppich & Stipek documented in California.
- CITE IT AS the first national-scale empirical treatment of superintendent leadership of ECE, and as evidence that superintendents report limited personal ECE background (6% ever taught Pre-K; 56% report no or limited ECE training). The background figures are among the least social-desirability-sensitive items in the instrument — there is little pressure to misreport whether you once taught Pre-K.
- DO NOT CITE the specific figure "62% of districts have no dedicated Pre-K staff member" as a national prevalence estimate. It is a proportion among 404 self-selected respondents at a 4% response rate, and the paper's own diagnostics show city districts — which are 26 percentage points more likely to centralize Pre-K leadership — are underrepresented. Cite it as "a majority of responding superintendents" or not at all.
- DO NOT CITE the sentence that these patterns "are evident nationwide" or that they "characterize superintendent leadership more broadly." The paper's own Methods section explicitly disclaims national representativeness; quoting the Discussion against the Methods misrepresents the study.
- DO NOT CITE the gender result as evidence that hiring more female superintendents would improve ECE implementation. The coefficient exists only for stated beliefs and disappears for both the efficacy composite and centralized organization — and women are overrepresented in the sample relative to the underlying superintendent population, so the variable is confounded with who chose to respond.
- DO NOT CITE the ECE-training coefficients as evidence that training changes superintendent priorities. The design is cross-sectional, selection into training is plausibly driven by preexisting ECE interest, and the estimates are non-monotonic (moderate training significant, extensive training not) in a way inconsistent with a dose-response mechanism. Cite it as a hypothesis the field should test, which is exactly how the paper frames it in Methods.
- DO NOT CITE the suburban result (-0.58 SD on the importance composite) as an established suburban Pre-K deficit. It is one exploratory coefficient among ~200, it sits alongside a *positive* suburban coefficient for ranking kindergarten readiness first, and its principal corroboration is the same author team's earlier single-state North Carolina principal study — which makes the two findings correlated evidence, not independent replication.
- DO NOT CITE any of the rank-battery coefficients as statements about how much superintendents value a given outcome. Ranks are compositional: raising literacy necessarily lowers something else. These coefficients describe relative ordering only.
- DO NOT CITE the favorable self-ratings of district ECE supports (including support to principals as ECE leaders) as evidence that those supports are adequate. These are superintendents grading their own districts, and the paper itself notes the ratings conflict with principal-perspective research.
- DO NOT USE this paper for any state-level or state-comparative claim. Nine states and DC returned zero respondents, California is underrepresented by 4.67 percentage points, and the authors explicitly restrict inference to pooled national analyses.
- USE IT AS a baseline and instrument source rather than as an effect-estimate source. The survey is available in the online appendix, and the highest-value use for a follow-on researcher is to re-field these items with a stratified or incentivized design that reaches a defensible response rate, and to triangulate against principals and ECE directors.
- OPEN QUESTIONS a reader should know remain unresolved: (1) whether any of the correlates survive a design that can rule out selection into the sample and selection into ECE training; (2) whether superintendent beliefs predict anything about actual district Pre-K quality, enrollment, or P-3 alignment — no outcome data of any kind appear here; (3) whether state Pre-K policy regime, entirely absent from the models, dominates the district-level and individual-level variation the paper does measure; (4) whether the favorable self-assessments hold up when principals and ECE directors in the same districts are asked.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Where this sits in the literature. The honest summary is that this paper converts a case-study literature into a descriptive national baseline, and that this is worth doing. Before it, the field's evidence on superintendents and ECE was three contemporary studies (Marietta's three-superintendent brief, Koppich & Stipek's 25 California interviews, Stein & Coburn's two California districts) plus two mid-1980s state surveys conducted when Pre-K largely sat outside public schools. Against that baseline, 404 superintendents drawn from a near-census national frame is a step change in scale even at a 4% response rate. The paper is now the best available evidence on its specific question — but that is partly a statement about how little competition it has. Readers should hold both facts at once: this is the reference point for superintendent ECE leadership, and the reference point is a descriptive survey with weak inferential purchase.

The central citation risk. The gap between quotable and supportable is unusually wide and unusually easy to characterize, because the paper writes both versions of the claim. Methods: findings "should be interpreted as reflecting patterns within this group of respondents rather than as representative of U.S. districts or superintendents nationally." Discussion, five pages later: the case-study dynamics "are not limited to particular states or communities but instead characterize superintendent leadership more broadly," and "these patterns are evident nationwide." The second formulation is what will end up in literature reviews, policy briefs, and AASA materials. It is not supported. The recommendation to readers is blunt: when this paper is cited for a nationwide generalization, check whether the citing text is quoting the Discussion against the Methods, and if so, downgrade.

Why the 4% rate matters more here than the paper's defense allows. The authors' defense rests on two moves: response rates are not reliable indicators of nonresponse bias (Hendra & Hill), and respondent districts look like national districts on CCD covariates. Both moves are legitimate as far as they go, and the diagnostics are more thorough than most papers bother with. But they address the wrong threat. The CCD gives enrollment, staffing, demographics, and locale; it does not give superintendent interest in early childhood education. The selection mechanism that should worry a reader is topic salience — a superintendent who has built a Pre-K program is measurably more likely to open and complete an email survey about Pre-K than one who has not — and that mechanism produces bias precisely in the direction of the paper's most-quoted level estimates: more support, more prioritization, more dedicated staffing, more perceived efficacy. Balance on district enrollment tells you nothing about it. This is why a sharp line is drawn in the guidance between the within-respondent contrasts (which survive) and the level estimates (which do not).

On the exploratory regressions. The paper's methodological self-awareness here deserves credit and it is worth being precise about what it does and does not buy. Calling the models exploratory, invoking Tukey and Lakens, saying that both null and significant results are tentative, and stating that the models are underpowered — this is the correct posture and it is stated repeatedly rather than buried in a limitations paragraph. What the posture does not do is change the arithmetic. Roughly 200 coefficients at alpha = 0.05 yields an expected 9-10 false positives, which is close to the number of starred coefficients the tables actually report. A reader cannot distinguish which of the significant coefficients are signal. The correct reading is that no individual coefficient in Tables 1-3 should update anyone's beliefs much, and that the tables collectively function as a menu of hypotheses for a future confirmatory study — which is exactly what the Limitations section says, and roughly the opposite of what the Discussion's narrative sections do with the training, gender, and suburban results.

The ipsative problem is underappreciated. Because Tables 1 and 2 model rank-ordered batteries, the outcomes within each table are mechanically constrained to sum to a constant. This means the coefficients within a battery are negatively coupled by construction, and the paper's flagship interpretive claim — that ECE-trained superintendents rank literacy lower and SEL higher, therefore training "helps superintendents align more closely with professional norms of the field" — is describing a single reallocation as though it were two independent findings pointing the same direction. It may still be a real and meaningful reallocation. But it is one fact, not two, and it says nothing about whether trained superintendents value literacy less in absolute terms.

What the paper genuinely establishes. Stripping away the overreach, three things survive and are worth the field's attention. First, the conceptual-versus-enacted support gap, which is well-measured because it is a within-respondent contrast. Second, the purposes ranking — superintendents see Pre-K as kindergarten preparation and as a special-education pipeline, and essentially never as family childcare infrastructure. That framing has downstream consequences the paper connects well to McCabe & Sipple and Wilinski on half-day scheduling. Third, that superintendents come to this work with thin ECE backgrounds, which is credible because those items are the least susceptible to social-desirability pressure in the instrument. These three claims are the ones a literature review can lean on.

A note on the follow-on agenda. The most valuable thing this paper produces may be the instrument itself, published in the online appendix. The field now has validated-by-cognitive-interview items for constructs nobody had operationalized. A researcher who re-fields these items with stratification, a serious incentive structure, and linkage to district Pre-K outcomes would supersede this paper — and would be able to do so quickly because the measurement work is done. The paper's own Limitations section essentially says this, and readers should take the authors at their word there rather than at the word of the Discussion.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

This published AERJ article documents its survey design, sampling frame, and nonresponse diagnostics unusually well and posts the instrument as Supplementary Appendix A, so the descriptive backbone is understandable and, in principle, re-fieldable. But it carries no data availability statement, no replication package, no code, no stated software environment, and no IRB/consent statement, and the regression machinery in Tables 1-3 is underspecified: the two standardized composite outcomes are never defined item-by-item, the ranking outcomes' coding direction is left implicit, per-model sample sizes and fit statistics are absent, the racial/ethnic composition controls are adjusted for but not printed, and every robustness check is described rather than shown. Readers can trust the descriptive findings as reported; the exploratory associations are effectively unverifiable from what is published.

**Strengths:**

- The sampling frame and fielding protocol are documented with unusual precision: the NLSD 2023-24 panel covering 12,572 K-12 districts, 10,031 publicly available superintendent emails (79.8%), 9,985 viable addresses (99.5%), an attempted census with no stratified subsampling, up to four reminder emails, a \$150 gift-card lottery incentive, Qualtrics administration in summer/fall 2024, and a 4% response rate calculated against AAPOR standard definitions. A replicator would know exactly what population was contacted and how.
- The survey instrument itself is deposited (Supplementary Appendix A, "the final version of the survey"), which is the single most important artifact for a survey paper and is more than many survey articles provide. Instrument development is also traceable: construct derivation from the literature, expert-panel review, and cognitive interviews with three current or former superintendents.
- Nonresponse and selection are interrogated across four appendices rather than waved off: Appendix B compares the 404 respondents to all U.S. districts on CCD enrollment, staffing, student demographics, and geography; Appendix C reports state-level response shares (42 states within +/- 2 pp; California under by 4.67 pp, Kansas over by 2.64 pp; nine states plus DC with zero respondents); Appendix D compares the 404 completers with the 28 partial completers; Appendix E describes the sample. The linking data source (NCES Common Core of Data) and the merged variable domains are named.
- Missing-data handling is stated explicitly and simply: "We analyzed data using the complete case data from the 404 superintendent respondents and therefore did not perform imputations or other missing data procedures." There is no ambiguity about whether imputation was used.
- The paper is candid about the epistemic status of its models, repeatedly framing them as exploratory conditional associations, disclaiming state-level inference, and warning that both null and significant coefficients are tentative. This honesty means a reader who cannot verify the models is at least not being asked to over-read them.

**Weaknesses:**

- No data availability statement, no replication package, no posted code, and no stated software environment. The back matter contains only "Supplemental material for this article is available online" alongside funding (Belk Foundation, Cornwell Foundation, IES) and conflict-of-interest declarations. Critically, these are the authors' own primary survey data, not restricted-use administrative records: nothing legal or contractual prevents depositing a de-identified respondent-level file with district identifiers coarsened, yet none is offered, not even "available upon request." For a 2026 journal article this falls short of current norms.
- The two standardized composite outcomes carrying the paper's headline associational claims (Model C, importance of Pre-K; Model D, district Pre-K efficacy) are never operationalized. The text says only "a standardized composite capturing the perceived importance of Pre-K in the district" and "a standardized composite capturing perceived efficacy and support for Pre-K leadership." Which of the Figure 4 and Figure 6 items enter each composite, whether items were averaged, summed, or factor-scored, whether reverse-coded items (e.g., the licensing-barriers item) were flipped, and what the internal consistency is (no alpha, omega, or factor analysis is reported anywhere) are all unstated. The 0.49 SD training coefficient, the 0.63 SD efficacy coefficient, the -0.35 SD male coefficient, and the -0.58 SD suburban coefficient therefore cannot be reconstructed even by someone holding the raw data.
- The models "also adjust for district student racial/ethnic composition" (identical note under all three tables) but those coefficients are never printed. This is not a cosmetic omission: Model E's substantive findings are entirely about them, with centralized Pre-K leadership reported as less likely as the multiracial share (-11 pp/unit) and American Indian share (-10 pp/unit) rise. Those two numbers appear in the narrative and in no table. The reader cannot see their standard errors, cannot confirm the significance stars, cannot tell which racial/ethnic categories were included, which was omitted as the reference, or whether the shares were entered on a 0-100 or 0-1 scale. The implausibly large and imprecise intercepts across all three tables (e.g., 25.25 with SE 20.57; 13.29 with SE 16.43; 9.88 with SE 5.86) strongly suggest the composition shares enter on a percentage scale and near-sum to a constant, exactly the situation where the unreported controls most affect interpretation.
- The rank-ordered outcomes in Models A and B cannot be rebuilt without guessing. The text describes coefficients as ranking a purpose "higher" by "+0.15 on the 5-point ranking scale" and outcomes by increments "of 6 points," implying the raw ranks were reversed so that larger values mean higher priority, but this recoding is never stated. Nor is it stated whether respondents had to rank all options, whether ties or partial rankings were permitted, how incomplete rankings were treated, or that the five purposes and six outcomes were each modeled as separate dependent variables (which induces mechanical negative dependence across columns that is never acknowledged).
- No sample size is reported for any regression model. Tables 1-3 give no N, no R-squared, and no fit statistics, and there is no statement that all 404 respondents enter every model. This matters most for Model E and the Pre-K leadership items generally, because the descriptive section makes clear these involve skip logic: roughly 38% of superintendents reported a dedicated ECE supervisor, and the 57% (on the senior leadership team), 81% (in regular district leadership meetings), and 59% (tasked with P-3 continuum work) figures are conditional on that subset. Whether Model E is estimated on 404 districts or on roughly 150 is unknowable from the paper, which in turn makes the +26 pp city coefficient impossible to situate.
- Model E's binary outcome is defined in prose as "there is a senior leader whose primary job responsibility is Pre-K, and they regularly attend senior leadership meetings," but the paper elsewhere uses two distinguishable items, membership on the superintendent's senior leadership team and attendance at regular district leadership meetings, with different prevalences (57% vs. 81%). Which item forms the second half of the conjunction is not pinned down, and the two choices would yield materially different outcome variables.
- The "training in ECE" predictor, which drives more significant coefficients than any other variable in the paper, has no reported item wording or response anchors in the main text. The four categories (none, limited, moderate, extensive) are self-classified with no definitional anchors given, and the main text reports only three of the four marginals: 14% none, 42% limited, 11% extensive, leaving "moderate" (the modal significant category in Table 3) to be inferred by subtraction at roughly 33%.
- Every robustness check is described but not displayed. Ordered logit re-estimates of Models A and B, logistic re-estimates of Model E, the full intercorrelation matrix, the variance inflation factors ("consistently <10"), and the sensitivity analyses adding and dropping correlated predictors such as percent Hispanic are all summarized as "substantively consistent" or "substantively unchanged," and none of the five named supplementary appendices (A instrument, B national comparison, C state response rates, D completers vs. non-completers, E sample descriptives) is said to contain them. These claims are pure trust.
- The item-level descriptive results, which are the paper's primary contribution, are presented only as figures (Figures 2-6) with no accompanying frequency tables or item Ns in the main text, despite the Analysis section stating that summary statistics were computed and tabulated for all survey items. Exact percentages must be read off bar charts. A concrete symptom: the Discussion reports that "83% of superintendents strongly agreed that Pre-K is critical to their district's educational success," but the Findings section reports only the combined 95% strongly agreed-or-agreed for that item. The 83% figure appears nowhere in the results and can only be checked against a figure's visual proportions.
- The NLSD sampling frame is a proprietary, lab-maintained resource with no documented access pathway. The paper describes its construction (CCD district list plus annually hand-collected superintendent names and contact information since 2019-20) and refers readers to White (2023a, 2023b) and White and Jerman (2025) for methodological detail, but gives no URL, request procedure, license terms, or cost. There is a legitimate privacy reason not to publish 9,985 individual email addresses, but the absence of any stated pathway means an outside replicator cannot reconstruct or even inspect the frame.
- No IRB or ethics approval statement and no description of informed consent, incentive administration, or respondent confidentiality protections appears anywhere in the article, which is both an ethics-reporting gap and part of why the absence of a de-identified data deposit cannot be evaluated on its merits.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat the descriptive findings (Figures 2-6 and the sample-composition statistics) as the verifiable core of this paper and the regression results (Tables 1-3) as provisional. The descriptives rest on a documented frame, a posted instrument, and a stated complete-case rule; the regressions rest on undefined composites and unprinted covariates. Cite the former with normal confidence and the latter only with the exploratory framing the authors themselves attach.
- Before citing any composite-outcome result, including the widely quotable "moderate ECE training predicts 0.49 SD higher perceived importance of Pre-K" and "suburban superintendents score 0.58 SD lower than rural," write to the corresponding author (mhlittle@ncsu.edu) for the exact item list, coding, and construction rule for the Model C and Model D composites, plus their reliability statistics. These effects are not reconstructible from the article, so their magnitudes are effectively uncheckable as published.
- Do not cite the Model E racial-composition findings (multiracial -11 pp/unit, American Indian -10 pp/unit) without first obtaining the full Table 3 including the suppressed racial/ethnic composition coefficients and their standard errors. These are narrative-only numbers with no printed uncertainty, no visible significance level, and no stated variable scale; the "/unit" phrasing is ambiguous between a one-percentage-point and a one-proportion change, and the two readings differ by a factor of 100. The authors themselves flag small base rates here.
- Request the per-model sample sizes before interpreting anything from Model D or Model E. The Pre-K leadership structure items are subject to skip logic (only about 38% of respondents reported a dedicated ECE supervisor, and the 57%/81%/59% statistics are conditional on that subgroup), so the effective N for the centralization model may be a fraction of 404. Combined with 14-plus predictors and the authors' own acknowledgment that the models are underpowered, an unstated small N would make the +26 pp city coefficient far more fragile than it appears.
- Ask for the undisplayed robustness output before relying on the linear-probability and OLS-on-ranks choices: the ordered logit re-estimates of Models A and B, the logistic re-estimate of Model E, the VIF table, and the drop-percent-Hispanic sensitivity runs. "Substantively consistent" is the only evidence offered, and OLS on a forced ranking with mechanically dependent columns is precisely the specification where an ordered model can diverge.
- Download Supplementary Appendix A and read the actual item wording before quoting any construct label. In particular, check the response anchors for the four-level ECE training measure (the paper's most productive predictor, with no anchors given in the main text), the ranking task's instructions (whether all options had to be ranked, whether ties were allowed), and the exact senior-leadership item used to build the Model E binary. Also retrieve Appendices B through E, since the entire nonresponse and representativeness case lives there and none of those numbers appear in the main text.
- Anyone attempting a full replication should plan on re-fielding rather than reanalyzing. No respondent-level data are posted, no code exists publicly, no software environment is named, and the NLSD frame is a proprietary University of Texas Superintendent Lab resource with no published access pathway. Contact the Superintendent Lab directly about frame access, consult White (2023a, 2023b) and White and Jerman (2025) for the database's construction, and budget for the fact that a 4% response rate on a near-census of about 10,000 addresses is what produced N = 404.
- Note two small internal inconsistencies when quoting figures and reconcile them against the exhibits or with the authors: the Discussion's "83% strongly agreed that Pre-K is critical" never appears in the Findings, which report 95% strongly agreed or agreed for that item; and the reported gender split (64.2% male, 35.9% female) sums to 100.1%. Neither undermines the paper, but both indicate that main-text percentages should be read off the figures rather than trusted verbatim.
- Read every claim in this paper as descriptive of 404 self-selected respondents, not of U.S. superintendents. The authors say so explicitly ("patterns within this group of respondents rather than as representative of U.S. districts or superintendents nationally"), and the two documented skews cut in directions that matter for this specific topic: female superintendents are overrepresented by roughly 7 percentage points relative to the NLSD population and are the group found to be most supportive of Pre-K, while city districts, which are the most likely to run Pre-K, are underrepresented. No weights were applied.
- If you need an ethics or data-governance basis for reuse (e.g., for a meta-analysis or an evidence synthesis with reporting standards), be aware the article contains no IRB approval statement, no consent description, and no data availability statement, so that information must be requested from the authors rather than cited from the paper.

**Detailed Commentary:**

The right way to characterize this paper's transparency is that its front end is strong and its back end is opaque. Everything about how respondents were reached is documented to a standard most survey articles do not meet: the frame is a named database with a construction history, the counts cascade transparently from 12,572 districts to 10,031 emails to 9,985 viable addresses to 404 completers, the response rate is computed against a named standard, the contact protocol and incentive are specified, and four separate appendices interrogate who responded relative to who did not. A reader can form an independent judgment about selection, which is exactly what a 4% response rate demands.

Everything about how the numbers were produced from those responses is much thinner. The paper's descriptive claims are largely traceable in the sense that each is tied to a quoted item stem and a percentage, though the percentages themselves live in figures rather than tables. The associational claims are not traceable. Two of the five outcome variables (the Model C and Model D composites) exist in the paper only as one-line noun phrases, with no item roster, no aggregation rule, and no reliability evidence. Two more (Models A and B) depend on an unstated rank reversal and unstated ranking-task rules. The fifth (Model E) is defined in prose using a phrase that maps ambiguously onto two distinct survey items with different prevalences. On the right-hand side, the covariate list is incomplete as printed, and the omission is not incidental, because Model E's only demographic findings are drawn from coefficients that were suppressed from the table. The oversized intercepts across all three tables are a visible tell that the suppressed controls are doing real work on a scale the reader cannot see.

What pushes this to weak rather than adequate is that none of this is forced by data constraints. Education research routinely earns leniency for restricted administrative data, and the NLSD contact frame genuinely cannot be published. But the analytic file here is 404 rows of the authors' own survey responses. A de-identified version with coarsened district identifiers, plus the estimation code, would resolve nearly every gap listed above and would cost the authors little. The article offers neither, offers no data availability statement explaining why, and does not even fall back on the weaker "available upon request." Combined with the absence of a stated software environment and of an IRB or consent statement, the transparency package is below what a 2026 AERJ article should carry.

What holds it above insufficient is that the study's actual contribution survives. The paper's own framing is that it is a national descriptive portrait, and the descriptive portrait is supported by a posted instrument, a documented frame, an explicit complete-case rule, and a serious nonresponse analysis. A reader can understand what was asked, of whom, with what response, and what the marginal answers were. It is the exploratory regression layer, which the authors themselves repeatedly discount, that is unverifiable. Confidence is high: this assessment is based on a text extraction without the five supplementary appendices, so it remains possible that Appendix A's instrument, once consulted, resolves the composite and ranking ambiguities, and it is possible the online supplement contains robustness tables the main text does not advertise. But the absence of a data availability statement, of any code, of per-model sample sizes, and of the racial/ethnic composition coefficients from the printed tables are all determinable from the main text alone, and no appendix would repair them.
